query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled low‐temperature aging treatment that induces homogeneous nano‐scale L12 precipitation within the FCC lamellae will improve the high‐temperature stability, suppress room‐temperature creep, and enhance corrosion resistance of the as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with a fine, uniform lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled low‐temperature aging (heat treatment) step after casting to trigger nano‐scale L12 precipitate formation in the FCC regions.
generation.conditions: Aging at a sub‐eutectic temperature (for example, between 600°C and 700°C) for a carefully determined time such that L12 precipitates form without coarsening the lamellar structure.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a uniform dispersion of nano‐scale ordered L12 precipitates within the FCC lamellae and more stable phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coherent L12 precipitates will act as additional obstacles to dislocation motion, thereby increasing yield strength and work hardening. Their presence is also expected to pin grain and phase boundaries, reducing microstructural coarsening and mitigating creep as well as potential corrosion pathways through stabilized interfaces under long-term mechanical loading and temperature fluctuations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as‐cast alloy, the aged alloy should exhibit an improved strength–ductility balance, enhanced resistance to room‐temperature creep and deformation under long-term load, and a more stable, less corrosive surface due to better-protected grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: The typical as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure that, while already showing a good strength and ductility combination, does not fully meet industrial high-temperature, long-term creep, and corrosion resistance requirements.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected provided aging is optimized; excessive aging may lead to precipitate coarsening or embrittlement. The improvement should hold for service environments up to about 700°C and under moderate corrosive conditions typical for aerospace fastener applications. Extremely severe conditions may require additional interventions.
generation.uncertainty: Exact aging temperature and duration and their quantitative effects on creep rate, corrosion resistance, and ductility need to be determined. It is also uncertain whether the induced precipitates will maintain their effectiveness over very long-term service or under more aggressive environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples. Subject one set to the controlled low‐temperature aging treatment (with variations in temperature and time within the defined window) and use as‐cast samples as controls. Test both sets under simulated service conditions that include long-term tensile or creep loading and cyclic temperature fluctuations. Additionally, perform standardized electrochemical corrosion tests to assess oxide scale stability and spallation.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation)
Creep tests under constant load at room temperature and elevated temperatures
Electrochemical corrosion measurements and oxide scale adhesion evaluations after thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., higher yield strength without excessive loss of ductility, reduced creep rates, and improved corrosion/oxide scale stability) over the as‐cast baseline—or if the treatment leads to notable embrittlement or precipitate coarsening—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD (calculation of phase diagrams) method can also provide an insightful guidance to design EHEAs, on the premise that reliable thermodynamics database for HEAs are to be established and completed. In summary, here we proposed a novel strategy to design high-entropy alloys (HEAs), i.e., the concept of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), to solve the challenging issues for this new type of advanced metallic materials, including the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility, and the inferior castability and compositional segregation. Based on the new strategy, we successfully designed a highly uniform AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, with an unprecedented combination of castability, high fracture strength and high ductility. The bulk EHEA ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared by the conventional casting method using the commercially pure raw materials. The EHEA exhibited a fine lamellar microstructure consisting of coupled grown fcc/B2 phases. Our design strategy is of great significance in both scientific and technical aspects, and can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs.

In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). A commonly adopted strategy to overcome this strength-ductility tradeoff is to develop multi-phase microstructures, involving at least one ductile/soft and one hard/strong phase, mixed in the appropriate proportion. Common examples include duplex alloys, such as 2205 stainless steel, which have a hard bcc phase to increase the strength of the alloy and a soft fcc phase to maintain the tensile ductility while deformation. The goal has been on fine-tuning the alloy composition and/or processing conditions in order to obtain a material with a good balance between ductility and strength. Eutectic alloys, often exhibiting a two-phase lamellar microstructure, offer such a possibility, and have been investigated for many years in different classes of alloys. Eutectic morphologies are characterized by the simultaneous growth of two (or more) phases from the liquid. A recently developed new class of eutectic HEAs (EHEAs), have attracted a lot of attention due to their promising mechanical properties.
